name: Esther Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a carpenter with Hollins Construction, and right now we're on a nine-storey rental block on the east side, by the old bus depot. I'm mostly on formwork, building the timber and ply moulds the concrete gets poured into, floor by floor. I'm on site by half six, kettle on in the cabin, then it's measuring, cutting, nailing and stripping last week's forms. I love the day a slab gets poured and the whole crew watches it go off clean. What wears me out is the cold and the rush when the pump truck is booked and we're not ready.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you spend your days with, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's six of us on the formwork crew. Kofi, who's been doing this thirty years, eats lunch with me on the pallets and tells me everything I'm doing wrong, kindly. At home it's me and Jonah, my partner, in a rented two-bed flat. Jonah drives the number 14 bus. We've got about three months of bills put by, which feels decent until the rent goes up again, and the landlord's already hinted it will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At work we'd laugh about it over tea, because the only AI anyone sees on site is the site manager's planning app that keeps getting the pour dates wrong. Online I'd probably share something about how the money went to tech bosses while the housing we actually need still gets built by people in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means the same worries I've got now, just without the robot ones on top. This block finishes in spring and Hollins hasn't said what's next. If there's a gap of six or eight weeks between jobs, that eats most of our savings with the rent where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do, and push the union rep to get the next contract sorted before this one ends. I'd put an extra fifty a week into savings over winter so a gap doesn't scare us. I'd ask Kofi which firms are hiring carpenters in the spring, because he always knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the robots, but not relaxed. The everyday stuff is still there, the rent and the gap between jobs. I'd sleep better than in the other pictures, put it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a gap between jobs. What gets cut first if it happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The takeaway on Fridays goes first, and the gym membership I barely use. Then we'd stop putting money aside for a holiday, which hurts, because Jonah's been talking about the coast for two years. The rent and the van insurance are the last things I'd let slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The labourers on day rates, mainly. They get let go the second a job finishes and they don't have a union card to fall back on. Robots or not, building work is feast or famine, and the people at the bottom feel the famine first.

say: I'd say **AI was hype**, and the only AI on site still gets pour dates wrong.
I'd post that the money went to **tech bosses** while **real housing** still needs builders in the rain.
think: Privately, my worries are the **same as now**: the block finishes in spring with no next job.
A **six-week gap** between contracts would eat most of our **three months** of savings.
do: Push the **union rep** to secure the next contract **before spring**.
Put an **extra fifty** a week into savings over the winter.
Ask **Kofi** which firms are hiring **carpenters** in the spring.
feel: **Relieved** that robots aren't coming, but still **not relaxed** about rent and gaps between jobs.
S0.quote: Robots or not, building work is feast or famine, and the people at the bottom feel the famine first.
fieldNote: Her main pressure is the **end of the contract**, not technology at all.
She quickly turned to **day-rate labourers**, showing a strong sense of who loses first.
She has a clear order of **what gets cut**, with rent and van insurance protected last.

steps.text: Keep building formwork on the east-side rental block until spring
Put an extra fifty a week into savings over winter
Press the union rep to line up the next contract early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office getting hit, not us, at least for now. You can't send an email to a sheet of ply and make it cut itself. I'd also say the firms should be made to keep people on and retrain them, not just pocket the savings, and I'd say that loudly at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the site office shrinks and we feel it sideways. If the estimator and the buyer get swapped for software, and the software gets something wrong, it's us on the deck waiting for timber that never got ordered. My actual hands stay busy, but I'd be working under people who know less about the job than the computer does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the formwork and keep my head down. I'd go to the union branch meetings, which I've been skipping, and back any push for rules on how firms use this stuff. I would not be signing up for any AI course, if I'm honest. I'd rather spend that evening getting my scaffold ticket, because that's a skill that stays in my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick, watching it happen to other people and knowing it's sliding towards us. I'm not panicking, because the hammer still matters. But I hate change I didn't ask for, and this is a lot of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather get a scaffold ticket than an AI course. Why that choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can see a scaffold and I trust it. My cousin Ruth (who works in an insurance office) did one of those AI courses and two months later her team got halved anyway. A scaffold ticket in my wallet is something nobody can automate away next Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonah that night, after the first big announcement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonah he's more at risk than me, because they've been testing driverless buses in the city centre for a year. We'd probably argue about whether he should do his HGV licence. Then we'd put the telly on and not talk about it.

say: I'd say the **office** gets hit first, because software can't cut a sheet of ply.
I'd tell the union meeting firms must **retrain staff**, not pocket the savings.
think: Privately, I think **ordering mistakes** from software would leave us waiting on the deck.
My hands stay busy, but I'd work under people who **know less** than the computer.
do: Go to **union branch** meetings and back rules on how firms use AI.
Get a **scaffold ticket** this year instead of any AI course.
Keep doing **formwork** with my head down.
feel: A bit **sick**, watching change slide towards her trade, though **not panicking** yet.
S1.quote: A scaffold ticket in my wallet is something nobody can automate away next Tuesday.
fieldNote: She **refuses AI training** on principle and chooses a hands-on ticket instead.
Her cousin's halved office team is her **proof** that courses don't protect anyone.
She sees her **partner's bus job** as more exposed than her own carpentry.

steps.text: Keep doing formwork for Hollins Construction
Attend union branch meetings and back rules on AI use
Get a scaffold ticket this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what the union warned about, and that the government let it happen with no plan. At work everybody would be shouting about it at lunch. Online I'd be sharing every petition going, because if there's no rules in two years there won't be any jobs in five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I've got until about 2031, and then I'm a 32-year-old carpenter with nothing else. The planning and ordering go first in 2028, so Hollins needs fewer site managers, but the robots that can do formwork come after. Three years sounds like a lot until you realise I don't know how to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent or food and try to get the savings from three months to six. I'd join every union action going, and I'd march. I'd probably look at whether Jonah and I could move back near my mum in the next couple of years, so if the robots come we're not paying city rent on no wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, mostly. Angry underneath that. I keep picturing the day a machine strips the forms my workmate Kofi taught me to build, and someone in an office I've never seen signs it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three years sounds like a lot. What would you actually do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save, mainly, and fight. I know that sounds stubborn, but I'm not going to become a coder at thirty. I'd look at the parts of building that are fiddly, like old-house repairs, because robots will be built for new sites first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Jonah's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah's buses would go before my carpentry, probably. So we could have both of us out of work within three years of each other. That's the bit that keeps me up, more than my own job.

say: I'd say the **union warned** about this and the government had **no plan**.
I'd share every **petition** online, because without rules **jobs disappear** in five years.
think: Privately, I've got until **about 2031**, then I'm a 32-year-old carpenter with **nothing else**.
Both of us could be **out of work** within three years, since driverless buses come first.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and push savings towards six months.
Join every **union action** and march for rules on robots.
Look at **moving near Mum** to escape city rent.
feel: **Frightened** first, with **anger** underneath about decisions made in offices she's never seen.
S2.quote: I keep picturing the day a machine strips the forms my workmate Kofi taught me to build, and someone in an office I've never seen signs it off.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year robot gap** as time to save and fight, not to switch.
Her real fear is **two lost incomes**, since her partner drives a bus.
She mentioned **old-house repair** as a hiding place, showing some quiet **planning** despite resistance.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and the van
Build savings from three to six months of bills
Join union marches and petitions for rules on robots
Look at moving near her mum to cut rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but I'd say we've got time to make rules this time, so no excuses. At the union I'd be pushing for a deal that says any robot on site comes with jobs kept or proper pay-offs. Online I'd be less shouty and more organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years plus three is 2034, and I'd be 35. That's long enough that I can't pretend it isn't coming, and short enough that I'll still need a job after it. The office side of Hollins changes by 2031, and then I've got a few years before the robots reach the deck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing formwork but start moving towards refurbishment and repair work, the old terraces round the market where every window frame is a different size. I'd save steadily, maybe a hundred a month more. And I'd get more active in the union, maybe stand as a site rep, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier than the fast one. There's room to breathe. I still don't like it one bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move towards refurbishment. Isn't that a change you'd normally avoid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I suppose it's still carpentry, still a saw in my hand, so it doesn't feel like jumping ship. I'd only do it if Kofi came along or I could learn from someone I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of this change your plans with Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about trying to buy a place in a few years. With driverless buses coming, I'd want to wait and see what happens to my partner's bus job before signing a mortgage. I'd rather rent a bit longer than owe a bank money I can't pay back.

say: I'd say there's **time for rules** this time, so politicians have no excuse.
I'd push the union for a deal: **robots on site** come with jobs kept or pay-offs.
think: Privately, robots reach the deck **around 2034**, when I'd be 35 and still need work.
The **office side** changes by 2031, so I'd watch Hollins thin out above me first.
do: Shift towards **refurbishment work** on old terraces where every frame differs.
Save about **a hundred more** each month.
Stand as a **site rep** for the union.
feel: **Worried** but **steadier** than in the fast picture, with some room to breathe.
S3.quote: With driverless buses coming, I'd want to wait and see what happens to my partner's bus job before signing a mortgage.
fieldNote: Five years makes her willing to **change direction**, but only within **carpentry**.
She'd **delay buying** a home, tying housing plans to her partner's **job risk**.
Union work shifts from protest to **organising**, including standing as **site rep**.

steps.text: Learn refurbishment work on old terraces from a trusted carpenter
Save about a hundred more each month
Stand as union site rep at Hollins
Delay buying a home until Jonah's bus job looks safe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so do it properly. Retraining paid for by the firms, rules on robots, pensions that don't vanish. I'd say that at work and at the union, and I'd probably bore my friends with it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be 39 when the robots come, which is the middle of my working life. Ten years makes me feel like I can put it off, and that's the danger with me, because I always put things off. I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for the first few years, honestly. Then I'd want to get into restoration carpentry, maybe a part-time college course in heritage joinery, once I see the first robot on a site. I'd keep saving and keep paying union dues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a slow way, like a damp patch you keep meaning to fix. It's not keeping me up yet. It would be by 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know you'd put it off. What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing one with my own eyes. If Hollins brought a robot onto a site and it did a day's formwork, I'd sign up for the heritage course that week. Until then it's just talk on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for yourself by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade the robots don't bother with, old buildings, odd jobs, churches, that kind of thing. And a home we own, so if the money goes thin we're not at a landlord's mercy. Jonah and I, maybe a dog, and my hands still doing the work.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to do this properly, so no excuses.
I'd call for **firm-paid retraining**, rules on robots and **pensions** that don't vanish.
think: Privately, robots arrive when I'm **39**, right in the **middle** of my working life.
Ten years tempts me to **put it off**, and I know I always do.
do: Carry on with **formwork** for the first few years.
Sign up for a **heritage joinery** course once a **robot** appears on site.
feel: A slow **unease**, like a **damp patch** she keeps meaning to fix.
S4.quote: Ten years makes me feel like I can put it off, and that's the danger with me, because I always put things off.
fieldNote: She openly names her **own habit** of delay as the biggest **risk**.
Her trigger for action is **seeing a robot** with her own eyes on site.
Long-term hope is **heritage carpentry** and a home they own.

steps.text: Keep doing formwork until a robot shows up on a site
Enrol in a part-time heritage joinery course
Keep adding to savings every month
Keep paying union dues and attending branch meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Not because of my job alone, but because Jonah's bus and my formwork could both go inside three years, with no time to plan. What would help is a union deal with real teeth, and the government paying for people like me to retrain in something solid, like heritage work, while still getting a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who builds the houses if the builders can't afford to live in them. Everybody talks about robots taking our jobs. Nobody talks about the rent going up while they do.

headlineQuote: Everybody talks about robots taking our jobs. Nobody talks about the rent going up while they do.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old formwork carpenter** on a rental block, living with her partner Jonah, a bus driver.
She's a committed **union member** who distrusts tech firms and never uses **AI tools**.
In mild pictures her worries are **rent** and **gaps between contracts**, not technology.
Fast AGI **alarms** her because both household incomes could vanish within **three years**.
Given time, she'd drift towards **heritage carpentry**, but admits she tends to **delay change**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her formwork job and Jonah's bus job could both go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** with real teeth on robots and job protection.
Government-paid **retraining with a wage**, in solid trades like heritage work.
